content: Late-onset neonatal sepsis, defined as a systemic infection occurring after 48 hours of age, remains a significant contributor to both morbidity and mortality in newborns. Prompt initiation of antibiotic therapy is critical, as neonates with suspected sepsis can experience rapid clinical deterioration. However, there is currently no consensus on the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen for treating suspected late-onset sepsis in this population. This review has been replaced by a more recent Cochrane Review (Korang 2021). The objective of the original review was to evaluate the efficacy and adverse effects of various antibiotic regimens used to treat suspected late-onset sepsis in neonates. The search strategy employed by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group included comprehensive electronic searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies published up to December 2004. Additionally, abstracts from Pediatric Academic Society meetings and references from previous reviews were examined. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared different initial antibiotic regimens in neonates with suspected late-onset sepsis. Two reviewers independently screened abstracts and full-text articles, assessed the methodological quality of the studies, and extracted relevant data. For dichotomous outcomes, treatment effects were expressed as relative risk (RR) and risk difference (RD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The number needed to treat (NNT) was calculated for outcomes with statistically significant reductions in risk difference. Thirteen studies were initially identified as potentially eligible for inclusion. However, most were excluded because they did not differentiate between early-onset and late-onset infections. Two studies remain under assessment. Ultimately, only one small study involving 24 neonates met the inclusion criteria. This study compared beta-lactam monotherapy with a combination of beta-lactam and aminoglycoside therapy. However, the study did not meet the predefined standards for methodological quality. In neonates with suspected late-onset sepsis, the study found no statistically significant differences in mortality (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.23) or treatment failure (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.23) between the two antibiotic regimens. Additionally, no cases of antibiotic resistance were reported in either treatment group. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from randomized trials to recommend any specific antibiotic regimen for the treatment of suspected late-onset neonatal sepsis. The available evidence is of low quality. Despite the frequent occurrence of suspected sepsis and the widespread use of antibiotics in neonates, high-quality research is urgently needed to evaluate the use of both narrow-spectrum and broad-spectrum antibiotics for late-onset neonatal sepsis. Future studies should also consider the cost-effectiveness of antibiotic regimens and their impact in various settings, including developed and developing countries, as well as in neonates of lower gestational ages.
